FADO: Learning Causal Explanations with Prior-Fitted Networks

Seth Flaxman ††thanks: Correspondence to seth.flaxman@rptu.de Affiliation: University of Oxford Affiliation: RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau    Jess Carr Affiliation: University of Oxford Affiliation: Ellison Institute of Technology    Annabel Jakob Affiliation: University of Oxford    Marek Masiak Affiliation: University of Oxford    Dino Sejdinovic Affiliation: Adelaide University
Abstract

In regression and classification tasks with tabular datasets, most of the literature on explanation in ML (e.g. SHAP, permutation importance) has focused on predictive attribution: does feature XiX_{i} help predict outcome YY? At its heart, predictive attribution captures correlation, not causation. We instead ask a causal question: would manipulating feature XiX_{i} change outcome YY? We define a natural quantity to answer this question, the feature intervention effect: Δi=E⁡[Y∣d​o​(Xi=+1)]−E⁡[Y∣d​o​(Xi=−1)]\Delta_{i}=E[Y\mid do(X_{i}=+1)]-E[Y\mid do(X_{i}=-1)]. In general, estimating this quantity from observational data alone would entail strong causal assumptions. We propose FADO (Feature-wise Amortized Do-Operators), an amortized inference method using prior-fitted networks trained on synthetic tabular datasets generated by structural causal models. During training, the synthetic data-generating process is known, so we can compute ground-truth intervention effects Δi\Delta_{i}, and train a model to predict them at test time from a purely observational tabular dataset. As we demonstrate through extensive experiments, our new causal explainability method is easy to train and provides better explanations under a range of settings for which standard predictive attribution fails, including proxy variables, confounders, colliders, and placebos. We evaluate it on real, synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets, with and without hidden confounders, and compare it to existing predictive attribution methods and state-of-the-art causal inference methods.

1 Introduction

When an ML model makes a high-stakes prediction in finance or healthcare, it is natural to ask “why?” and demand an explanation (Goodman and Flaxman, 2017). Indeed, the EU’s new AI Act (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024) contains an article, effective August 2026, on the “Right to Explanation of Individual Decision-Making” laying out a right to “clear and meaningful explanations” from deployers of AI systems in high-risk settings. The extensive ML literature on explainability aims to answer the question “why did the model make this prediction?”

While these model-based predictive attribution questions are of course incredibly important, machine learning is increasingly entering many scientific domains, including natural science and social science. Here, a related but distinct question arises: which variables would change the outcome if they were intervened upon? By contrast, model-based predictive attribution asks: does a given feature help predict the outcome? In scientific domains, it is often the data-generating process from nature itself that is the object of study, rather than a specific predictive model, so an explanation should answer “what if” questions about interventions (Pearl, 2009), rather than associational questions about a model’s predictions. In practice, predictive attribution methods give qualitatively different information from causal inference methods (see fig. 1) and we expect disagreements between the two methods to be particularly useful for practitioners to interrogate, as they could point towards non-causal associations driving model predictions.

Here, we focus on tabular datasets and view causal explanation through the lens of feature intervention effects: feature-wise interventional contrasts that ask how the outcome would change on average under an intervention on a particular predictor. Estimating this contrast for each feature yields a new causal feature-importance ranking, where importance reflects the effect of manipulating that feature in the data-generating process rather than its usefulness for predicting YY. It can be used alongside or instead of popular predictive attribution methods like SHAP.

Existing explainability methods are usually post-hoc: a model is fit and then explained. By contrast, we use prior-fitted networks (PFNs) and amortization to learn to predict causal explanations directly from underlying data-generating processes. This approach is in line with a philosophy of “learning to explain” (Situ et al., 2021). Building on a recent series of papers on causal inference with PFNs (Robertson et al., 2025b; Balazadeh et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Robertson et al., 2025a) we demonstrate empirically that this approach is robust when trained on a sufficiently diverse set of priors. The training process is very simple: we sample a tabular dataset from a data-generating process, calculate the vector of feature intervention effects, which we term the causal feature profile, and then use supervised learning, training a transformer to predict the causal feature profile from the tabular dataset.

Predictive vs. causal attribution.

Figure 1 illustrates the difference between predictive and causal attribution with five motifs, each a small structural causal model (SCM). In motif A, X1X_{1} is a direct cause of YY. In motif C, X2X_{2} is a mediator on the path from X1X_{1} to YY. In the other three motifs, the highlighted feature is associated with YY but has no causal effect on it: in motif B, X1X_{1} co-varies with YY only through their observed common cause ZZ; in motif D, X1X_{1} is caused by YY; and in motif E, the collider CC is caused by both X1X_{1} and YY. The right panel plots each highlighted feature’s TreeSHAP importance under a LightGBM predictor (section 5.2) against FADO’s estimated intervention effect τ^\hat{\tau}. We call a feature predictive if its TreeSHAP importance is high, and causal if its true intervention effect is nonzero. The direct cause X1X_{1} in motif A and the mediator X2X_{2} in motif C are both predictive and causal. The descendant X1X_{1} in motif D and the collider CC in motif E are predictive but not causal, and FADO assigns them τ^≈0\hat{\tau}\approx 0. The confounded X1X_{1} in motif B is neither predictive nor causal, since the predictor also sees ZZ. Finally, the upstream X1X_{1} in motif C is causal but not predictive, because its effect on YY is carried entirely by X2X_{2}, and FADO detects it. Predictive attribution tells a user which features a model uses for predictions, while causal attribution tells a user which features to intervene on. Manipulating X1X_{1} in motif D or CC in motif E would leave YY unchanged. X1X_{1} in motif C has low TreeSHAP importance for predicting YY, but manipulating it would have a large causal effect. Section 5.2 compares predictive baselines with ground-truth intervention effects on held-out SCMs, and section 5.4 applies a standard TreeSHAP workflow to a real randomized marketing dataset, where it highlights an outcome leak.

Contributions.

  • •

    We introduce the feature intervention effect τi\tau_{i} (eq. 2) as a per-feature quantity for causal explanations, closely related to average treatment effects and dose-response curves (table 1). It can be used to understand the impact of intervening on individual features, and to rank feature importance causally.

  • •

    We introduce a supervised learning framework called “learning to explain” and develop FADO (section 3) for learning causal explanations, based on amortized inference over a large class of synthetic data generating processes (table 20), and train a foundation model (table 21) to predict a vector of feature intervention effects from a tabular dataset.

  • •

    We demonstrate that our method is effective, giving qualitatively different measures of variable importance versus existing predictive attribution methods (figs. 1, 15 and 5.4) and highly efficient (appendix M), fast enough to run as an interactive demo in a web browser (https://mlgh.net/fado-demo/) on tables of up to 64 features (appendix C).

  • •

    We theoretically analyze FADO, showing that squared-loss training leads to a Bayes optimal posterior mean (proposition 1).

FADO’s aim is to output an accurate feature importance ranking based on causal interventions, reliably identifying causal features and zeroing out non-causal features. While we compare to causal discovery methods, our goal is not accurate point estimation of the causal effect for a specified treatment. Instead, we aim to simultaneously explain all features at once.

2 Setup and Target Functional

Let X=(X1,…,Xp)∈ℝpX=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{p})\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and Y∈ℝY\in\mathbb{R} be the observed variables of a structural causal model (SCM) MM, with possible additional latent variables, and let GG denote its directed acyclic graph (Pearl, 2009; Hernán and Robins, 2020). For each feature i∈1,…,pi\in 1,\ldots,p we define the raw feature intervention effect as the causal effect on YY using do-operators:

Δi​(M)=𝔼M​[Y∣do⁡(Xi=bi)]−𝔼M​[Y∣do⁡(Xi=ai)]\boxed{\Delta_{i}(M)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{M}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(X_{i}=b_{i})]-\mathbb{E}_{M}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(X_{i}=a_{i})]} (1)

We define the standardized feature intervention effect as:

τi​(M)=Δi​(M)σY​(M),\boxed{\tau_{i}(M)\;=\;\frac{\Delta_{i}(M)}{\sigma_{Y}(M)},} (2)

where σY​(M)\sigma_{Y}(M) is the standard deviation of YY under MM’s observational law. For all features we use the standardized (±1)(\pm 1) contrast (ai,bi)=(−1,+1)(a_{i},b_{i})=(-1,+1)11 1 Input features are standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Balanced binary features are thus ±1\pm 1, matching the convention of dividing inputs by 2​σ2\sigma before reading off coefficients (Gelman, 2008). In linear settings, the choice of (ai,bi)(a_{i},b_{i}) is irrelevant, but nonlinear mechanisms could be sensitive to this choice. We conduct a sensitivity analysis in appendix Q and find no meaningful change in the ranking of causal effects, and only small changes in the magnitude of the effects.

Our goal is to learn the entire pp-dimensional vector causal feature profile τ⁡(M)=(τ1​(M),…,τp​(M))\tau(M)=(\tau_{1}(M),\ldots,\tau_{p}(M)). We write τ^​(Dn)\hat{\tau}(D_{n}) for FADO’s prediction of τ\tau given an observational table Dn={(xr,yr)}r=1nD_{n}=\{(x_{r},y_{r})\}_{r=1}^{n}, and τ^i\hat{\tau}_{i} for its ii-th coordinate.

3 Architecture and Training

We train a transformer (section 3.1) on a mixture of 1111 SCM prior families (section 3.2) for 150,000150{,}000 steps with squared loss (section 3.3); the noise distribution of each column is drawn from seven families (section J.1). The resulting foundation model, FADO (Feature-wise Amortized Do-Operators), takes datasets with between 33 and 1515 features and extends to 6464 features in appendix C.

3.1 Axial Transformer

FADO treats observations as an exchangeable set, in the style of Lee et al. (2019), and alternates attention along the two axes of the table, following Somepalli et al. (2022). Given a dataset D∈ℝn×(p+1)D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(p+1)} where column p+1p+1 is YY, FADO returns the full causal feature profile τ^∈ℝp\hat{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} in a single forward pass. Each scalar cell is projected to a dd-dimensional embedding, and a learned type embedding with two values (“feature” and “target”) is added to break the symmetry between features and target. The embeddings then pass through 66 layers, each of which applies two post-norm multi-head attention blocks (Vaswani et al., 2017): feature axis attention, in which the p+1p+1 cells of a row attend to each other, and sample axis attention, in which the nn cells of a column attend to each other. After the last layer, the cell embeddings are averaged over samples within each column, and a linear readout at the pp feature positions produces τ^∈ℝp\hat{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}. FADO uses d=384d{=}384 and 88 heads (14.214.2M parameters).

3.2 SCM Prior Families

Each training SCM is drawn from one of 1111 prior families, summarized with their relative weights in table 20 (appendix J). The families span linear, polynomial nonlinear, hidden confounder, and mixed-type settings. In the four families with linear mechanisms (linear, hidden confounder, and the two mixed-type families), the labels are computed in closed form (section R.2). As a special case, under no confounding (no open backdoor paths; ignorability), τi​(M)=2​Corr⁡(Xi,Y)\tau_{i}(M)=2\,\operatorname{Corr}(X_{i},Y) (section R.3). In the other seven families, τi​(M)\tau_{i}(M) is estimated by Monte Carlo: ndon_{\mathrm{do}} samples are drawn from the post-intervention SCM and averaged for each value of the intervention.

For each column jj, the distribution of the noise εj\varepsilon_{j} is drawn uniformly from seven families, independently across columns (section J.1).

3.3 Training Protocol

Data generation.

FADO is trained on synthetic datasets generated from the SCM priors described in section 3.2. Each training step samples a batch of BB SCMs from the prior, simulates nn rows from each, and applies a random column permutation with the labels permuted accordingly. So that a single model can handle datasets with different numbers of features, datasets with fewer than 1515 features are padded to 1515 with columns of independent standard normal noise whose τ\tau label is 00, and the columns are permuted a second time so that the padding can appear at any position. At inference, datasets are padded the same way and the predictions at the padding columns are discarded.

Training objective.

The model parameters are optimized to minimize the squared loss on τ^−τ\hat{\tau}-\tau. To improve training stability, we apply several guards: τ\tau is clamped to [−5,+5][-5,+5]; batches with any non-finite label are skipped; and the gradient norm is clipped to 1.01.0.

Optimizer and hyperparameters.

FADO is trained with the AdamW optimizer, a cosine schedule, learning rate 10−410^{-4} and a 5,0005{,}000-step linear warmup. For the single-family comparisons in sections 5.1 and N we also train smaller models, each on one prior family. These single-family variants use learning rate ×10−43\!\times\!10^{-4} with a 200200-step warmup and Laplace noise in every column, except for two controls with Gaussian noise, where causal direction is not identifiable (section 4.3). Hyperparameters for all models are given in table 21 (appendix J).

4 Theory: What FADO Learns

FADO is a prior-dependent amortized estimator of a causal functional in eq. 2. The pretraining simulator defines a distribution over SCMs and provides intervention labels for each sampled SCM. At test time, the input is only an observational table, so the relevant population target is determined by the posterior over SCMs induced by the pretraining prior and that table. This section formalizes the target functional, shows that squared-loss pretraining identifies the posterior mean of the causal feature profile, and characterizes when that posterior mean converges to the true profile versus a prior-weighted average over observationally equivalent SCMs.

4.1 Pretraining Prior and Target Functional

Let 𝔐\mathfrak{M} be a class of SCMs whose observed variables are (X1,…,Xp,Y)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{p},Y), possibly together with additional latent variables. Let M∼ΠM\sim\Pi denote the pretraining prior over 𝔐\mathfrak{M}. The observational law induced by MM on the observed variables is PMP_{M}, and an observational table of nn rows is

Dn={(xr,yr)}r=1n∼PMn.D_{n}=\{(x_{r},y_{r})\}_{r=1}^{n}\sim P_{M}^{n}. (3)

Assume 0<VarM⁡(Y)<∞0<\operatorname{Var}_{M}(Y)<\infty throughout. The causal feature profile τ⁡(M)=(τ1​(M),…,τp​(M))∈ℝp\tau(M)=(\tau_{1}(M),\ldots,\tau_{p}(M))\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is defined component-wise by eq. 2; the standardization puts all labels on the same outcome scale. We note that the causal feature profile is equivariant to relabeling of the feature columns (derivation in section R.1), and the estimator of τ\tau constructed in Section 3 respects this equivariance property of the target by construction.

4.2 Bayes-Optimal Amortized Predictor

Consider the population squared-loss risk over measurable maps f:𝒟n→ℝpf:\mathcal{D}_{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{p},

ℛ2​(f)=𝔼M∼Π​𝔼Dn∼PMn​[‖f⁡(Dn)−τ⁡(M)‖22].\mathcal{R}_{2}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{M\sim\Pi}\mathbb{E}_{D_{n}\sim P_{M}^{n}}\left[\|f(D_{n})-\tau(M)\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (4)
Proposition 1 (Bayes action for the causal profile).

Assume 𝔼Π​‖τ⁡(M)‖22<∞\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\|\tau(M)\|_{2}^{2}<\infty. Any population minimizer of eq. 4 satisfies

fΠ⋆​(Dn)=𝔼Π​[τ⁡(M)∣Dn]almost surely.f_{\Pi}^{\star}(D_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\!\left[\tau(M)\mid D_{n}\right]\qquad\text{almost surely.} (5)

Moreover, if the pretraining prior is invariant under relabeling of the feature columns, in the sense that M∼ΠM\sim\Pi implies Mπ∼ΠM^{\pi}\sim\Pi for every permutation π\pi, then

fΠ⋆(Dnπ)j=fΠ⋆(Dn)π⁡(j),j=1,…,p,almost surely.f_{\Pi}^{\star}(D_{n}^{\pi})_{j}=f_{\Pi}^{\star}(D_{n})_{\pi(j)},\qquad j=1,\ldots,p,\qquad\text{almost surely.} (6)

Equation 5 shows that FADO is a PFN-style causal estimator (Müller et al., 2022; Robertson et al., 2025b; Balazadeh et al., 2025): it is an amortized estimator of the Bayesian posterior mean of the causal profile functional, where the posterior is induced by a pretraining prior. It does not directly recover “the” causal effect unless the posterior over SCMs assigns the same causal feature profile to all observationally plausible SCMs. Equation 6 states that an invariant pretraining prior induces an equivariant posterior-mean target, which agrees with the equivariance of the true causal profile. Therefore, column order should not carry information during pretraining. We can enforce this by column-permuting the synthetic SCMs (and corresponding labels). This motivates the design choices in the transformer architecture (Section 3), in which computation is shared across feature columns and the model outputs one coordinate per feature, so that relabeling input features relabels output effects.

4.3 Identifiability of the Feature Profile

Fix a data-generating SCM M0M_{0} with observational law P0=PM0P_{0}=P_{M_{0}} and causal profile τ0=τ⁡(M0)\tau_{0}=\tau(M_{0}), and let Dn∼P0nD_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n}. Write Πn(⋅)=Π(⋅∣Dn)\Pi_{n}(\cdot)=\Pi(\cdot\mid D_{n}). The feature profile is identifiable at M0M_{0} under Π\Pi if τ⁡(M)=τ0\tau(M)=\tau_{0} for every observationally equivalent MM (i.e. every MM in the prior support with PM=P0P_{M}=P_{0}). This is weaker than identifying the full graph or the full SCM: observationally equivalent SCMs may differ structurally while agreeing on the causal feature profile. Under three regularity conditions (formal versions in section R.4) – (A1) posterior consistency for the observational law, (A2) local continuity of τ⁡(M)\tau(M) in PMP_{M} at P0P_{0}, and (A3) a bounded-profile condition – the posterior mean of τ⁡(M)\tau(M) converges to τ0\tau_{0}. (A2) is the key identifiability assumption.

Proposition 2 (Consistency under local profile identifiability).

If (A1)–(A2) hold, then, for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0,

Πn​{M:‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2>ϵ}→0in ​P0n​-probability.\Pi_{n}\{M:\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}>\epsilon\}\to 0\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}. (7)

If, in addition, (A3) holds, then

fΠ⋆​(Dn)=𝔼Π​[τ⁡(M)∣Dn]→τ0in ​P0n​-probability.f_{\Pi}^{\star}(D_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\tau(M)\mid D_{n}]\to\tau_{0}\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}. (8)

Equation 7 states that learning the observational law is sufficient to learn the causal feature profile when the local continuity holds. Equation 8 then gives consistency of the posterior mean which in turn corresponds to the population optimizer of eq. 4. Note that the result concerns the population optimizer induced by the pretraining prior, it does not address the optimization error of a finite trained network. Section R.7 illustrates both regimes empirically on an identifiable prior (linear non-Gaussian) and a non-identifiable prior (linear Gaussian, where the direction of edges cannot be determined from observational data). Section R.8 studies non-identifiable regimes showing that the posterior mean converges, under regularity, to the prior-weighted mean of the causal profiles compatible with P0P_{0} and that the risk is lower bounded by the residual variation in τ⁡(M)\tau(M) among observationally equivalent SCMs.

Where the prior helps.

The identifiability status depends on the structural class. In unrestricted SCM classes, observational equivalence with different intervention effects is common (Pearl, 2009; Hernán and Robins, 2020). In purely Gaussian linear SCMs, causal direction is generally not identified from observational covariance alone. In linear non-Gaussian acyclic models with independent errors, the graph and total effects are identifiable under LiNGAM assumptions (Shimizu et al., 2006). In nonlinear additive-noise models, causal direction is generically identifiable only under additional asymmetry conditions (Hoyer et al., 2008). These results explain why a prior dominated by non-Gaussian SCMs can learn a useful causal profile from observational samples. Gaussian and hidden-confounder SCMs fall outside these guarantees, so we evaluate them separately.

Summary.

FADO learns the Bayes action for τ⁡(M)\tau(M) under the SCM pretraining prior, which is the posterior mean 𝔼Π​[τ⁡(M)∣Dn]\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\tau(M)\mid D_{n}]. With finite data, this averages the causal profiles of SCMs weighted by their posterior probability given the table. As n→∞n\to\infty, it converges to the true causal profile when that profile is identifiable within the prior. Otherwise it converges to an average over observationally equivalent SCMs weighted by the prior alone (section R.8).

5 Experiments

We evaluate FADO on an extensive battery of synthetic and real datasets, and compare it with state-of-the-art causal inference and predictive attribution methods (section 5.2). The evaluations cover held-out SCMs and motif stress tests (section 5.1), real covariates with synthetic outcomes (section 5.3), and real RCTs with constructed proxy, leak and noise decoys (section 5.4). The appendix adds the Sachs DAG (appendix D), uncertainty analysis (appendix G), architecture ablations (appendix E), cross-family generalization (appendix N) and timings (appendix M).

5.1 Held-Out Random SCMs

We evaluate FADO on held-out random SCMs from each of its eleven prior families (table 20). Each family contributes 200200 SCMs with p=5p{=}5 features padded to 1515, nrows=512n_{\mathrm{rows}}=512 samples, and the per-column noise of section J.1. We report Pearson rr with the true τ\tau, AUROC for nonzero-feature detection, and MAE on zero-effect features (table 2), pooled across the features of all 200200 SCMs, with a marginal-correlation baseline (τ^i=2⋅Corr⁡(Xi,Y)\hat{\tau}_{i}=2\cdot\mathrm{Corr}(X_{i},Y)) as a non-causal reference. The same FADO model is used in every row. Smaller single-family variants, each trained and evaluated on one family, are compared in appendix B.

On five motifs (fig. 1; A: direct cause, B: observed confounder, C: mediator, D: target descendant, E: collider), FADO assigns τ^≈0\hat{\tau}\approx 0 to non-causal predictive features (B/D/E) while predictive baselines find non-zero effects; per-motif paired-bootstrap CIs and per-baseline behaviour are in table 15 (appendix F).

Cross-family generalization (appendices N and 5), seed stability (table 7), a heterogeneous-pp single model on p∈[3,15]p\in[3,15] (table 8), and a scatter of τ^\hat{\tau} vs τ\tau (fig. 4) are reported in appendix B.

5.2 Predictive Attribution and Causal Inference Baselines

We compare FADO against three families of baselines on 500500 held-out SCMs per regime, summarized in table 3. Causal discovery methods (DirectLiNGAM (Shimizu et al., 2006), NOTEARS (Zheng et al., 2018), PC (Spirtes and Glymour, 1991), GES (Chickering, 2002), and FCI (Spirtes et al., 1995)) return a causal graph, from which τ^\hat{\tau} is computed via A=(I−B)−1A=(I-B)^{-1} (section R.2). Per-column treatment effect estimators (Double Machine Learning (Chernozhukov et al., 2018) and Causal Forest (Athey et al., 2019), both doubly-robust by construction) are designed for a known treatment, so we apply them per-column with each feature playing the treatment role in turn. Predictive attribution baselines (marginal correlation, linear regression, permutation importance, and path-dependent TreeSHAP via LightGBM) answer a predictive rather than an interventional question. We include them to quantify the difference between predictive and causal importance on a causal target. We also compare with Do-PFN and CausalPFN (Robertson et al., 2025b; Balazadeh et al., 2025). These methods require designating a single binary treatment column so the evaluation is not entirely fair: we binarize and use them one feature at a time (appendix K).

FADO outperforms every other method on every column of table 3, except where LiNGAM’s identifiability assumptions (linear non-Gaussian, no hidden confounders) hold. We also compare FADO with do-Shapley (Jung et al., 2022), a Shapley-value attribution of interventional effects that must be given the true SCM. FADO, which sees only the observational table, beats it on three of five families, while do-Shapley is better on the two hidden-confounder families (table 9 in appendix B).

To evaluate FADO and other methods’ ability to zero out non causal features, we construct a diverse suite of real and semi-synthetic experiments, including RCTs, physical systems (appendix H), and synthetic decoys with real covariates.

5.3 Semi-Synthetic Experiments: Real Covariates

We test FADO on real covariates with simulated outcomes. We take the covariates of the ACIC-2016 benchmark (Dorie et al., 2019), 48024802 rows of 5858 features from a real study, sample 88 columns per dataset, and simulate an outcome from them, so that every column’s τ\tau is known. We created 40 SCM instances per outcome family: linear, mixed nonlinear, and interaction. We consider four types of decoys: (1) a proxy variable is correlated with a true causal predictor; (2) a leak variable is a function of the outcome variable; (3) a pure noise variable is independent of the other variables; and (4) a confounder child variable is a noisy copy of a hidden confounder. In all cases, the true τ\tau for these decoy variables is 0. We considered two regimes: no confounding and hidden confounders. We calculated false positives as mean |τ^||\hat{\tau}| at decoy positions; lower is better.

Our findings are in table 4. FADO assigns nearly zero effect to pure-noise decoys (below 0.010.01), as does multivariate regression. FADO assigns smaller effects than marginal correlation to every decoy type, and it is the best method on the outcome leak in every setting. Multivariate regression assigns the smallest effects to proxies and confounder children, because conditioning on the true causes absorbs them, but it gives the outcome leak a large effect.

5.4 Real RCTs with Constructed Decoys

Section 5.3 uses real covariates with simulated outcomes. Here we use real outcomes. The Hillstrom e-mail marketing experiment (Hillstrom, 2008) randomly assigned customers to receive a men’s merchandise e-mail or no e-mail, and recorded whether they visited the website. We augment its pre-treatment covariates and treatment TT with the same kinds of constructed decoys as in section 5.3: a proxy PTP_{T} correlated with TT, a leak LY=Y+εL_{Y}=Y+\varepsilon, and three pure-noise columns. FADO sees the augmented covariates {X,T,PT,LY,noise}\{X,T,P_{T},L_{Y},\mathrm{noise}\} and YY, with no indication of which column is the treatment. Success is defined as FADO estimating an effect for TT that matches the sign and magnitude of the RCT estimate, and estimating effects of approximately zero for PTP_{T}, LYL_{Y} and the noise columns.

On the augmented Hillstrom feature matrix, we fit a LightGBM on {X,T,PT,LY,noise}\{X,T,P_{T},L_{Y},\mathrm{noise}\} and report path-dependent TreeSHAP via LightGBM’s pred_contrib (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020) on visit outcome22 2 The choice of SHAP method is irrelevant in this case, because Janzing et al. (2020)’s “interventional SHAP equals do-calculus” result holds only under a flat causal graph in which every feature is a root node. See appendix O.. This conclusion is not specific to the SHAP variant used: all variants we test behave alike on our benchmarks (appendix O). The classifier AUC is 0.9980.998, driven entirely by the leak column LYL_{Y}, which SHAP scores as the most important feature. FADO also assigns LYL_{Y} a large effect (τ^=+1.03\hat{\tau}=+1.03, 95%95\% CI [+0.67,+1.32][+0.67,+1.32]), as does DR-Learner (Kennedy, 2020), run per-feature with RandomForest first/second/final stages and 2-fold cross-fitting (τ^=+1.08\hat{\tau}=+1.08, [+1.06,+1.09][+1.06,+1.09], ∼30×\sim 30\times its largest other estimate). On the true (hidden) treatment FADO under-shoots (−0.01-0.01, [−0.06,+0.09][-0.06,+0.09]) consistent with the magnitude shrinkage discussed in section 7. Per-feature estimates and bootstrap CIs are in table 26 (appendix P).

We further test on 124124 real RCTs from RCT Bench (Shao et al., 2026), a public collection of participant-level trial data. We run FADO on each trial’s covariates and treatment, without decoys, and compare its estimate for the treatment column, τ^T\hat{\tau}_{T}, with the trial’s difference in means. Though not designed for this task, FADO attains a correlation of 0.850.85 with ground truth. CausalPFN, specifically designed for this task, achieves 0.960.96.

5.5 Uncertainty Quantification

We quantify FADO’s uncertainty with 100100 random bootstrap resamples, reporting feature-wise standard deviation σi\sigma_{i} of τ^i\hat{\tau}_{i}. Though confidence intervals are not calibrated (table 16), they do track error: Spearman correlation between σi\sigma_{i} and |τ^i−τi||\hat{\tau}_{i}-\tau_{i}| ranges from 0.650.65 to 0.900.90 across regimes (table 17), and leaving out the most uncertain features sharply reduces error, both on a physical system and on real covariates with simulated outcomes (fig. 3).

6 Related Work

Our work is situated in multiple literatures: explainability, causal inference and causal discovery, amortized inference, and prior-fitted networks. We mention foundational papers and those that are directly relevant to our approach. Permutation importance (Breiman, 2001; Fisher et al., 2019) along with SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Jethani et al., 2022) are widely adopted predictive attribution approaches, focused on explaining the predictions of a fitted model rather than the data-generating process. A method with an overlapping spirit to ours is learning to explain (L2E) (Situ et al., 2021), which trains a network to predict explanations directly, targeting a predictive rather than interventional functional.

Causal inference is a long-standing area within statistics (e.g. (Holland, 1986)), social science (e.g. (Morgan and Winship, 2014)), and epidemiology (e.g. (Hernán and Robins, 2020)), with a related and very rich literature on causal discovery in computer science (e.g. (Pearl, 2009; Spirtes et al., 2001; Bühlmann et al., 2014; Peters et al., 2017)). Causal discovery takes a dataset and returns a causal graph. A separate, deep literature on per-unit treatment effect estimation (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Athey et al., 2019; Kennedy, 2020; Hill, 2011) targets (conditional) average treatment effects for a user-designated treatment, whereas FADO returns a length-pp vector of per-feature intervention contrasts in a single forward pass, with no designated treatment.

Prior-fitted networks (PFNs) (Müller et al., 2022) amortize Bayesian inference by training a model on synthetic datasets sampled from a prior, so that the trained network performs inference in-context at test time. For tabular data this paradigm is typified by TabPFN (Hollmann et al., 2025) and causal inference using PFNs has seen much recent work (Robertson et al., 2025b; Balazadeh et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Robertson et al., 2025a). Causal Articulation Theory (Zečević et al., 2026) is complementary to our work, because it can produce natural language explanations from FADO’s output.

7 Limitations

FADO learns the Bayes posterior mean of τ⁡(M)\tau(M) under the prior. Thus, its accuracy in matching the true causal feature profile depends on whether that profile is identifiable from tabular observational datasets (section 4.3, A1–A3). For example, FADO’s performance suffers under linear Gaussian and hidden confounder data generating processes (table 3) because observational datasets under this prior are consistent with multiple causal structures. We found that FADO provides a reliable feature ranking and identifies causal vs. non-causal features (including zeroing proxy/noise decoys), but it does not accurately predict point estimates of effect sizes. While the paper’s main FADO model is trained on tables of up to 15 features, we extend training to 64 features in appendix C.

8 Conclusion

We introduced a new method, FADO, motivated by the increasing use of machine learning in scientific domains, where predictive attribution methods are useful but can mislead on their own. We hope FADO becomes a default, baseline method for causal explanations, responsive to “what if?” questions, phrased interventionally. FADO’s implementation requires amortized inference through prior-fitted networks, building on the exciting “learning to explain” framework, which could be relevant for many application domains and types of data beyond tabular.

Appendix B Held-out Random SCMs: Extended Results

Table 5 compares FADO with smaller single-family variants (table 21), each trained on one prior family and evaluated on 500500 held-out SCMs from that family. Every row is therefore an in-distribution evaluation, and rows are not directly comparable. All rows use Laplace noise in every column, except the Gaussian control. The FADO row evaluates the FADO model on linear SCMs under this protocol. It is higher than the linear row of table 2 (0.990.99 against 0.950.95 in Pearson rr), which uses FADO’s per-column noise of section J.1. Table 6 adds further variants: the Linear p=5p{=}5 variant at 1515k steps, the two Large architecture variants (d=192d{=}192, 4+4 layers, part of the architecture sweep in appendix E), the Gaussian control at p=8p{=}8, MLP ++ hidden confounder, and the p=13p{=}13 replicates of the hidden-confounder and mixed-type families. All results in the paper use the FADO model except the tables comparing model variants (tables 5, 6, 8, 11 and 21).

We compare do-Shapley, which has access to the true graph, to FADO, which does not (table 9).

Appendix C Wider Tables

The FADO foundation model of the main text is trained on tables with p∈[3,15]p\in[3,15] features, padded to 1515 columns. Nothing in the architecture depends on pp (section 3.1), so the same network can be trained on wider tables. We trained two further models with the same architecture, optimizer, step count and prior families as table 21, differing only in how table width enters training:

  • •

    FADO p≤64p{\leq}64. Following the width scheme of TabPFN (Hollmann et al., 2025), each training step draws a single width p∼LogUniform⁡[3,64]p\sim\mathrm{LogUniform}[3,64] and samples a batch of SCMs at that width, with no padding. The number of rows per table is capped so that n⁡(p+1)≤16,384n\,(p{+}1)\leq 16{,}384 cells; at p=64p{=}64 this still allows the full n=512n{=}512 rows. Gradients are accumulated over two half-batches to fit the widest tables in 4040 GB of GPU memory. Training took 77.777.7 h on one A100 (3.3×3.3\times the p≤15p{\leq}15 model, whose cost scales roughly linearly in pp).

  • •

    FADO p≤64p{\leq}64, fixed density. Identical, except that the graph prior holds the expected number of parents per node fixed as pp grows. The prior of table 20 draws each earlier-to-later edge independently with probability 0.350.35 (0.400.40 for the MLP and GP families), so the expected in-degree is about 2.52.5 at p=15p{=}15 but 5.55.5 at p=32p{=}32 and 1111 at p=64p{=}64, and the fraction of features with a nonzero effect stays near 0.40.4. For p>15p>15 this variant scales every family’s edge probability by 14/(p−1)14/(p{-}1) (to 0.1580.158 at p=32p{=}32 and 0.0780.078 at p=64p{=}64), which keeps the expected in-degree at its p=15p{=}15 value, as TabPFN and TabICL (Qu et al., 2025) do by holding graph density independent of width. For p≤15p\leq 15 the prior is unchanged. Training took 3636 h on one L40S.

Table 10 evaluates all three models on 500500 held-out mixture-prior SCMs at p∈{15,32,64}p\in\{15,32,64\} with n=512n{=}512 rows and the heavy-tailed per-column noise of section J.1, under both the paper’s graph density and the fixed density. The same 500500 SCM draws are used for every model within a setting (fixed seed), so columns are paired. The p≤15p{\leq}15 model is applied unpadded at p>15p>15; it has never seen a table wider than 1515 columns.

Training on tables of up to 6464 features does not reduce accuracy at p=15p{=}15, and the resulting model beats the p≤15p{\leq}15 model at every wider setting (table 10). The p≤15p{\leq}15 model still works beyond its training width: at p=64p{=}64 on fixed-density graphs it reaches Pearson rr of 0.690.69, against 0.450.45 for the marginal baseline. Under the paper’s density, p=64p{=}64 is hard for every model: each node has eleven parents in expectation, and the best model barely beats predicting zero in MSE. On fixed-density graphs of the same width, both models recover most of their p=15p{=}15 accuracy. A padded p∈[3,32]p\in[3,32] control, trained with the main text’s recipe, does about as well at p=32p{=}32 under the paper’s density (r=0.64r{=}0.64 against 0.620.62 for the p≤64p{\leq}64 model).

Holding the graph density fixed during training did not help. The fixed-density model is worse than the p≤64p{\leq}64 model in every row of table 10, including at p=15p{=}15, where the two training priors are identical (rr of 0.730.73 against 0.820.82; seed-to-seed variation of the p≤15p{\leq}15 model is about 0.0050.005), and it is worse than the p≤64p{\leq}64 model even on the fixed-density evaluation graphs it was trained on (0.680.68 against 0.760.76 at p=64p{=}64). One possible explanation is that a sparse wide table has few nonzero effects, so most of its labels are zero and it carries less training signal. The browser demo (appendix A) uses the p≤64p{\leq}64 model trained on the paper’s density.

Appendix D Sachs Published DAG

We take the DAG structure (1111 nodes, 1717 edges) from Sachs et al. (2005)’s protein-signaling network and populate its edges with 3030 random draws of linear non-Gaussian coefficients. Across all feature draws, every model variant beats marginal correlation (table 11).

Appendix E Architecture Ablations

We retrained the foundation model from scratch three times, each time removing one component and keeping every other setting (150150k steps, same prior, seed 00), and evaluated each like the full model: 200200 held-out linear SCMs at p=5p{=}5 padded to 1515 columns.

Without feature axis attention or the type embedding (the only signal distinguishing the YY column from feature columns), the model learns nothing; without sample axis attention it still learns, but less accurately (table 12).

Inference-time type-flip diagnostic (table 13): the retrain ablation could in principle reflect the model relying on the fixed position-pp readout convention rather than on the type embedding signal. Holding the foundation model fixed, we re-evaluate on the same held-out set after substituting the type-id vector passed to the type-embedding lookup. With all-zero or mis-pointed type IDs, Pearson rr collapses (table 13). The position-pp convention carries no signal at inference time, so we concluded that the trained model relies on the type embedding to identify the target column.

Appendix F Motif Specifications and Results

The five handcrafted DAG motifs used in section 5.1 stress prototypical predictive-vs-causal failure modes: each motif has a “key feature” (coloured in fig. 1) which is non-causal but predictive in B/D/E (so τ=0\tau=0 despite high marginal correlation with YY), and both causal and predictive in A/C. We evaluate FADO and baselines on 5050 random-coefficient instances of each motif, reporting the mean τ^\hat{\tau} across instances with paired-bootstrap 95%95\% confidence intervals (table 15). FADO correctly assigns near-zero τ^\hat{\tau} to the non-causal but predictive features in B, D, and E, while marginal correlation reports a strong effect on these features. Multivariate regression and SHAP succeed on B, where conditioning on the observed confounder ZZ removes the spurious signal, but they fail on D and E, where the spurious feature is downstream of YY and not in the conditioning set.

Appendix G Uncertainty: Coverage and Estimator Comparison

Appendix H Causal Chambers: Real Physical Interventions

We evaluate on the light tunnel device of the Causal Chambers (Gamella et al., 2025). This physical system is accompanied by a causal graph, in which every actuator can be independently set, with ground truth effects measured directly from experiments. We use the uniform reference experiment (n=10,000n{=}10{,}000); ground truth τ\tau is computed at μ±σ\mu\pm\sigma from the intervention data. Table 18 reports per-feature results for the vis1\mathrm{vis}_{1} configuration, whose sensor decoys (e.g. ir2\mathrm{ir}_{2}, correlation 0.900.90 with the outcome, true τ=0\tau=0) are near-deterministic functions of several actuators.

Because the chamber randomizes every actuator, there is no confounding and regression recovers the effects accurately. Thus, this method serves as a sanity check on whether methods can avoid attributing effects to non-causal passive sensors. TreeSHAP ranks a non-causal sensor ir2\mathrm{ir}_{2} most highly, while a backdoor adjustment using the published graph correctly suppresses it. FADO also assigns these sensors nonzero mass because they are almost deterministic functions of the actuators, but FADO’s uncertainty measure flags exactly these columns (section 5.5).

Appendix I Semi-Synthetic Real-XX (UCI covariates)

In this experiment, we test FADO on real covariates XX with synthetic outcomes Y=f⁡(XC)+εY=f(X_{C})+\varepsilon generated by a known SCM with a designated causal subset of features CC. We inject the same proxy / leak / noise decoys as in section 5.4 to isolate the real-covariate-distribution effect from the real-outcome effect. We achieve this property since τ\tau is known by construction and the held-out Pearson rr and decoy false-positive rates remain well-defined. We test five settings: diabetes and california_housing each crossed with {linear, mixed nonlinear} outcome, plus abalone with an interaction outcome (30 SCM instances per setting). We evaluate FADO on each setting.

The results are summarized in table 19. In the linear-outcome settings, the multivariate regression baseline wins the Pearson rr column as expected since it’s the correct model, but it collapses on the mixed nonlinear settings. Moreover, FADO assigns smaller spurious effects to the decoys than marginal correlation does, except on one noise column where both are near zero.

Appendix J Architecture and Training Details

  • •

    Layers: each layer applies feature axis attention (within each row, the p+1p{+}1 cells attend to each other) and then sample axis attention (within each column, the nn cells attend to each other), using post-norm transformer blocks with feed-forward factor 22. Width, heads and number of layers for each model are in table 21.

  • •

    Value projection: single linear layer ℝ→ℝd\mathbb{R}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{d} applied per cell of D∈ℝn×(p+1)D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(p+1)}.

  • •

    Type embedding: learned ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} vector added to the value embedding; feature columns share one type, the YY column has the other.

  • •

    Readout: the final cell embeddings are averaged over samples within each column, then a linear layer ℝd→ℝ\mathbb{R}^{d}\!\to\!\mathbb{R} is applied at feature positions.

  • •

    Training cost on one H100: ≈0.37\approx 0.37 s/step, 1515 h for the 150150k steps of the foundation model.

J.1 Per-column noise families

The FADO foundation model draws the noise family independently per column. For each feature column jj, a family is sampled uniformly from the seven listed in table 22, the raw values are drawn with the indicated parameters, and the column is then centred to mean 00 and rescaled to unit sample variance. The post-hoc rescaling matters for the families whose parametric variance depends on a random shape parameter (signed log-normal, bimodal Gaussian mixture). Across a pp-feature SCM, different columns therefore typically have different marginal shapes.

Appendix K Using Interventional PFNs as Per-Feature Causal Estimators

We compared our method to CausalPFN (Balazadeh et al., 2025) and Do-PFN (Robertson et al., 2025b). However, neither of these models were designed for the estimation of feature intervention effects. To apply them, we designate each feature as the treatment variable, one by one, and ask the interventional PFNs to estimate a causal effect. More specifically, for each setting and each feature column j∈{1,…,p}j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:

  • •

    median-binarize XjX_{j} to a {0,1}\{0,1\} pseudo-treatment so it matches the binary-TT prior baked into both released models;

  • •

    treat the remaining p−1p-1 columns of XX as the conditioning set, which includes downstream descendants of XjX_{j}, violating the pre-treatment-covariates assumption of both priors;

  • •

    for CausalPFN, call ATEEstimator on (X∖j,X~j,Y)(X_{\setminus j},\tilde{X}_{j},Y); for Do-PFN, swap XjX_{j} into column 00 of DobD^{\mathrm{ob}} and integrate the predicted conditional interventional distribution to obtain ATE^j=𝔼⁡[Y∣do⁡(X~j=1)]−𝔼⁡[Y∣do⁡(X~j=0)]\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_{j}=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(\tilde{X}_{j}{=}1)]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(\tilde{X}_{j}{=}0)] averaged over rows (the canonical Do-PFN-CATE reduction);

  • •

    rescale to per-σ\sigma-XjX_{j} units for comparability with FADO’s standardized contrast.

CausalPFN and Do-PFN perform similarly in this setting and require similar overhead. FADO returns all pp effects in a single forward pass. For timings, see appendix M. Both the CausalPFN and Do-PFN runs were performed on a single RTX 5000 Ada, with total compute under 1010 minutes across all 88 settings.

Appendix M Per-Call Wallclock Comparison

FADO, as an amortized method, returns all pp per-feature effects in a single forward pass (∼\sim1 ms on GPU regardless of p∈{5,13}p\in\{5,13\}), while per-feature CATE estimators (DoubleML, Causal Forest) scale linearly in pp because each feature triggers an independent fit/inference. LightGBM-SHAP, DoubleML, Causal Forest pays the per-dataset training cost on every new dataset.

The FADO foundation model (last row of table 21, 14.214.2M parameters) trained in ∼15\sim 15 h 1818 min on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU (≈367\approx 367 ms/step over 150,000150{,}000 steps; three seeds at 55,07755{,}077 s, 55,13655{,}136 s and 55,11655{,}116 s). The single-family variants in table 21 (1515k–5050k steps) are far cheaper: the largest, Linear p=5p{=}5 at 5050k steps, trained and was evaluated in 5959 min on one H100. Per-call timing reported in table 25 is the median of 2020 repetitions on fresh linear non-Gaussian SCMs at nrows=512n_{\mathrm{rows}}{=}512 (Causal Forest at p=13p{=}13 CPU was capped at 55 repetitions for budget; all other cells use 2020).

“inference” rows pay only a forward pass per dataset. “fit ++ explain” rows include training the per-dataset estimator (LightGBM regressor; LinearDML / CausalForestDML per feature) on the input table before producing attributions.

At p=13p{=}13, FADO on GPU is roughly 1,100×1{,}100\times faster than Causal Forest on CPU at producing the length-pp contrast vector.

Appendix N Cross-Family Generalization

Our main FADO model is trained on a mixture prior. As a sensitivity analysis, we investigated single-family ablations. In fig. 5 we consider 88 p=5p{=}5 model variants (the 77 single-family p=5p{=}5 variants in tables 5 and 6 plus FADO). On the diagonal, where train and evaluation families match, performance is high, but off-diagonal performance does not drop too drastically. The mixture foundation FADO model outperforms single family models. The Gaussian evaluation column is the hardest, which makes sense from theory.

Appendix O SHAP Variants and the Predictor-to-SCM Gap

Table 1 summarizes how the causal feature profile τ\tau relates to existing per-feature quantities used for attribution and explanation: each estimator answers a different question, and only τ\tau is an interventional contrast.

The distinction between interventional and conditional SHAP is important for explaining a fitted predictor, but it does not by itself identify the SCM that generated the data. Janzing et al. (2020)’s “interventional SHAP is consistent with do-calculus” claim is a claim about the input distribution of the predictor ff: equivalently, about a flat causal graph 𝒢flat\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{flat}} in which every feature is a root node and there are no edges between features. Under 𝒢flat\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{flat}}, marginal sampling of X−SX_{-S} and do⁡(XS=xS)\mathrm{do}(X_{S}{=}x_{S}) coincide, so the marginal-baseline expectation 𝔼⁡[f⁡(xS,X−S)]\mathbb{E}[f(x_{S},X_{-S})] is a well-defined do-quantity.

That flat graph is generally not the real SCM that produced the training data. When the true mechanism has X2=g⁡(X1)+εX_{2}=g(X_{1})+\varepsilon, marginal-sampling X2X_{2} while holding X1X_{1} fixed can produce (X1,X2)(X_{1},X_{2}) pairs that occur in no observational or interventional distribution under the SCM (Janzing et al., 2020; Aas et al., 2021). Sundararajan and Najmi (2020) compare the BShap, RBShap and CES variants. Their analysis concerns the predictor’s input model and does not provide a way to recover SCM-level edges from observations of ff alone. Aas et al. (2021) likewise frame the interventional-vs-conditional choice as a question about feature dependence in the observational distribution, not about identification of the data-generating mechanism.

These variants all perform predictive attribution for the fitted model, rather than causally explaining the data-generating process. Shapley methods that do target the data-generating process, such as do-Shapley, require the causal graph (table 9). The choice among these variants also makes little difference in our experiments: path-dependent TreeSHAP, interventional TreeSHAP, and kernel SHAP agree closely on held-out SCMs (Pearson rr within 0.050.05–0.090.09 of one another across five families), and all three assign the outcome leak their largest decoy score (0.370.37–0.700.70; true τ=0\tau=0). Counterfactual Shapley values (Lee et al., 2026) are defined with respect to a known SCM rather than a fitted predictor, so there is no data-only implementation to compare to. The variants can be faithful to their respective predictive targets (𝒢flat\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{flat}} or the observational manifold) while still answering a different question from the interventional feature effect τi\tau_{i}.

Appendix Q Anchor Audit: Is the (−1,+1)(-1,+1) Contrast a Faithful Summary?

FADO returns a single per-feature scalar τ^i\hat{\tau}_{i} trained to match the symmetric population contrast Δi​(−1,+1)=𝔼⁡[Y∣do⁡(Xi=+1)]−𝔼⁡[Y∣do⁡(Xi=−1)]\Delta_{i}(-1,+1)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(X_{i}=+1)]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(X_{i}=-1)]. This anchor pair has a known degeneracy: for any mechanism that is even-symmetric in XiX_{i} around the origin (e.g. Y=Xi2+εY=X_{i}^{2}+\varepsilon), Δi​(−1,+1)≡0\Delta_{i}(-1,+1)\equiv 0 even though intervening on XiX_{i} does move YY. We check whether this affects five real datasets: Hillstrom, LaLonde, Criteo, Sachs and Tübingen.

Method.

Per feature XiX_{i} in each dataset, no model retraining:

  • •

    Standardize XiX_{i} to zero mean / unit variance and YY likewise.

  • •

    Estimate r^i​(t)=𝔼^​[Ystd∣Xi,std=t]\hat{r}_{i}(t)=\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{\rm std}\mid X_{i,\rm std}=t] at the fixed grid t∈{−2,−1,0,+1,+2}t\in\{-2,-1,0,+1,+2\} via Nadaraya-Watson with a Gaussian kernel (bandwidth 0.40.4 in standardized XX units), and an effective-sample-size guard neff​(t)≥25n_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)\geq 25 to keep heavy-tail outliers from dominating any single anchor.

  • •

    In parallel, compute a rank-based crosscheck r^i​(F−1​(q))\hat{r}_{i}(F^{-1}(q)) at q∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}q\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}. Each rank bin has equal sample count by construction, so the rank-based summary is robust to heavy tails.

  • •

    Flag feature XiX_{i} when both |Δ^i​(−1,+1)|≤0.05|\hat{\Delta}_{i}(-1,+1)|\leq 0.05 and maxq⁡r^i​(F−1​(q))−minq⁡r^i​(F−1​(q))≥0.20\max_{q}\hat{r}_{i}(F^{-1}(q))-\min_{q}\hat{r}_{i}(F^{-1}(q))\geq 0.20. Two-sided in standardized YY units.

The audit is observational. r^i\hat{r}_{i} estimates 𝔼⁡[Y∣Xi=t]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X_{i}=t], not 𝔼⁡[Y∣do⁡(Xi=t)]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(X_{i}=t)]. Confounding biases the symmetric contrast and the curve range identically, so the comparison is unaffected; a flagged feature is not necessarily a flagged causal effect.

Result.

Across the five real datasets, 33 of 149149 feature-level audits flag the symmetric-contrast blind spot (table 27).

The three flagged cases have non-monotone observational shapes. Two are inverted-U and one is a threshold at the negative tail:

  • •

    Criteo f2. Rank-based curve (−0.21,−0.21,+0.46,+0.13,−0.20)(-0.21,-0.21,+0.46,+0.13,-0.20). |Δ^f​2​(−1,+1)|=0.031|\hat{\Delta}_{f2}(-1,+1)|=0.031, rank range 0.680.68. An asymmetric anchor pair (+0.5,+1.5)(+0.5,+1.5) already shows −0.32-0.32. The curve drops above the median. The covariate is anonymised, so we make no causal claim, only that its observational shape is not symmetric.

  • •

    Tübingen pair0024. Gaussian-anchor curve (+0.59,−0.08,−0.12,−0.06,−0.05)(+0.59,-0.08,-0.12,-0.06,-0.05). Threshold-like at the negative tail: only the lowest-XX bin produces a non-trivial response. |Δ^​(−1,+1)|=0.021|\hat{\Delta}(-1,+1)|=0.021, rank range 0.270.27.

  • •

    Tübingen pair0094. Gaussian-anchor curve (−0.37,−0.09,+0.33,−0.07,−0.27)(-0.37,-0.09,+0.33,-0.07,-0.27). Inverted-U. |Δ^​(−1,+1)|=0.015|\hat{\Delta}(-1,+1)|=0.015, rank range 0.810.81.

Figure 6 plots |Δ^i​(−1,+1)||\hat{\Delta}_{i}(-1,+1)| against the rank-based curve range over all 149149 feature audits, colour-coded by dataset; the flag region is the shaded strip on the left. Most features sit on or above the y=xy=x line: symmetric contrast and rank-based range agree, i.e. the effect is monotone and the symmetric pair captures it. Sachs is the clearest case. Every protein lies far from the flag region because the benchmark SCM is linear by construction. Tübingen, despite being curated for nonlinear cause-effect relationships, mostly contains monotone-nonlinear pairs (saturating, log-link), which the symmetric pair handles fine; only the non-monotone pairs are flagged.

Reading the result.

This is mostly a negative result and we frame it as such.

  • •

    The symmetric-contrast head Δi​(−1,+1)\Delta_{i}(-1,+1) is a defensible default on the datasets in this paper: ≈97%\approx 97\% of feature audits across 55 datasets show no blind spot.

  • •

    The known degeneracy on symmetric nonlinear mechanisms does occur in practice, but rarely. We found three instances in 149149 audits. When it does occur, the pattern is a peak-and-decay or threshold shape.

  • •

    A natural extension is to widen the head from a single anchor pair to a KK-anchor curve readout r^i​(tk)\hat{r}_{i}(t_{k}) at tk∈{−2,−1,0,+1,+2}t_{k}\in\{-2,-1,0,+1,+2\}, of which the existing Δi​(−1,+1)\Delta_{i}(-1,+1) is one entry. We do not pursue this in the present paper because the empirical incidence here is too low to motivate the extra parameters; we flag it as the right next step when a target dataset shows Criteo-f2- or pair0024-style structure.

Appendix R Further Details on Theoretical Results

R.1 Equivariance of the causal feature profile

The causal feature profile is equivariant under relabeling of feature columns. Let π\pi be a permutation of {1,…,p}\{1,\ldots,p\}, and write MπM^{\pi} and DnπD_{n}^{\pi} for the SCM and dataset with features relabeled by Xj′=Xπ⁡(j)X^{\prime}_{j}=X_{\pi(j)}, leaving the outcome YY unchanged. Then

τj​(Mπ)=𝔼M​[Y∣d​o​(Xπ⁡(j)=bπ⁡(j))]−𝔼M​[Y∣d​o​(Xπ⁡(j)=aπ⁡(j))]σY​(M)=τπ⁡(j)​(M).\tau_{j}(M^{\pi})=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{M}[Y\mid do(X_{\pi(j)}=b_{\pi(j)})]-\mathbb{E}_{M}[Y\mid do(X_{\pi(j)}=a_{\pi(j)})]}{\sigma_{Y}(M)}=\tau_{\pi(j)}(M).

The estimator constructed in section 3 respects this equivariance by construction.

R.2 Linear continuous SCM closed-form label

For the linear continuous SCM family, the causal feature profile admits a closed-form label. Let Z=(Z1,…,Zp+1)Z=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{p+1}) collect the observed variables, with feature XiX_{i} corresponding to node ziz_{i} and outcome YY corresponding to node yy. Suppose

Z=B​Z+E,Z=BZ+E, (9)

where Bj​kB_{jk} is the coefficient from parent kk to child jj, and let A=(I−B)−1A=(I-B)^{-1}. If the intervention levels (ai,bi)(a_{i},b_{i}) are expressed in standardized units of XiX_{i}, then the standardized outcome contrast is

τi​(M)=(bi−ai)​Ay,zi​σXiσY.\tau_{i}(M)=(b_{i}-a_{i})\,A_{y,z_{i}}\,\frac{\sigma_{X_{i}}}{\sigma_{Y}}. (10)

For the families with nonlinear mechanisms, τi​(M)\tau_{i}(M) is estimated by Monte Carlo draws from the post-intervention SCM (section 3.2).

R.3 Reduction to marginal correlation

We note that eq. 10 reduces to marginal correlation in the exogenous one-feature linear case. Let XiX_{i} and YY be population-standardized to unit variance, with the contrast (ai,bi)=(−1,+1)(a_{i},b_{i})=(-1,+1), and

Y=βi​Xi+ηi,𝔼⁡[Xi​ηi]=0.Y=\beta_{i}X_{i}+\eta_{i},\qquad\mathbb{E}[X_{i}\eta_{i}]=0.

Equivalently, the only contribution to the covariance between XiX_{i} and YY is the total linear effect of XiX_{i} on YY; in the single-edge case Xi→YX_{i}\to Y, this total effect is the direct coefficient βi\beta_{i}. Then Ay,zi=βiA_{y,z_{i}}=\beta_{i} and Corr⁡(Xi,Y)=Cov⁡(Xi,Y)=βi\operatorname{Corr}(X_{i},Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{i},Y)=\beta_{i}, so

τi​(M)=2​Corr⁡(Xi,Y).\tau_{i}(M)=2\,\operatorname{Corr}(X_{i},Y).

We use marginal correlation as a baseline in section 5.2. It will only recover the correct causal effect under the assumptions of exogeneity and linearity, while it will fail under confounding, reversed direction, target-descendant leakage, collider or selection effects, etc.

R.4 Formal assumptions and technical preliminaries

This subsection collects formal definitions and assumptions referenced informally in section 4. Notation matches that section: M0M_{0} is a data-generating SCM with observational law P0=PM0P_{0}=P_{M_{0}} and causal profile τ0=τ⁡(M0)\tau_{0}=\tau(M_{0}); Dn∼P0nD_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n}; Πn(⋅)=Π(⋅∣Dn)\Pi_{n}(\cdot)=\Pi(\cdot\mid D_{n}).

Bounded Lipschitz metric.

We metrize weak convergence of observational laws on 𝒵=ℝp+1\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{R}^{p+1} by the bounded Lipschitz metric

dBL​(P,Q)=sup‖h‖∞≤1,Lip⁡(h)≤1|∫h​𝑑P−∫h​𝑑Q|.d_{\mathrm{BL}}(P,Q)=\sup_{\|h\|_{\infty}\leq 1,\ \operatorname{Lip}(h)\leq 1}\left|\int h\,dP-\int h\,dQ\right|. (11)

Effective prior support and equivalence classes.

Let 𝔐Π\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi} denote an effective prior support, with Π⁡(𝔐Π)=1\Pi(\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi})=1 and Πn​(𝔐Π)=1\Pi_{n}(\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi})=1 for P0nP_{0}^{n}-almost every DnD_{n}. The observational equivalence class of P0P_{0} inside this support is

ℰΠ​(P0)={M∈𝔐Π:PM=P0}.\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}(P_{0})=\{M\in\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi}:P_{M}=P_{0}\}. (12)

The feature profile is identifiable at M0M_{0} under Π\Pi if τ⁡(M)=τ0\tau(M)=\tau_{0} for all M∈ℰΠ​(P0)M\in\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}(P_{0}). This is weaker than identifying the full graph or the full SCM: observationally equivalent SCMs may differ structurally while agreeing on the causal feature profile.

Identifiability assumptions (A1)–(A3).

(A1) Observational posterior consistency.

Let P∙:𝔐→𝒫⁡(𝒵)P_{\bullet}:\mathfrak{M}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}) denote the map M↦PMM\mapsto P_{M}. Then

(P∙)#​Πn⇒δP0in ​P0n​-probability.(P_{\bullet})_{\#}\Pi_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{P_{0}}\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}. (13)

where ⇒\Rightarrow denotes weak convergence of probability laws on 𝒫⁡(𝒵)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Z}).

(A2) Local continuity of the profile.

For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that

dBL​(PM,P0)<δ⟹‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2<ϵ,M∈𝔐Π.d_{\mathrm{BL}}(P_{M},P_{0})<\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}<\epsilon,\quad M\in\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi}. (14)
(A3) Bounded profile.

There exists B<∞B<\infty such that

‖τ⁡(M)‖2≤Bfor all ​M∈𝔐Π,‖τ0‖2≤B.\|\tau(M)\|_{2}\leq B\quad\text{for all }M\in\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi},\qquad\|\tau_{0}\|_{2}\leq B. (15)

(A1) is a standard posterior consistency condition for observational laws which typically holds in well-specified models under Kullback–Leibler support and testing conditions. (A2) is the key identifiability assumption: continuity of the causal profile at M0M_{0} when SCMs are compared through their observational laws. (A3) is a boundedness condition used to pass from posterior concentration of τ⁡(M)\tau(M) to convergence of posterior means; it is imposed for simplicity and can be weakened to posterior uniform integrability.

Equivalence-class disintegration.

Assume the prior admits a regular conditional distribution over SCMs given their observational law, restricted to the effective support 𝔐Π\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi}, and write

ΠP0(⋅)=Π(⋅∣PM=P0).\Pi_{P_{0}}(\cdot)=\Pi(\cdot\mid P_{M}=P_{0}).

Let QΠ,P0=τ#​ΠP0Q_{\Pi,P_{0}}=\tau_{\#}\Pi_{P_{0}} be the induced distribution of causal feature profiles among SCMs observationally equivalent to P0P_{0}.

(A4) Equivalence-class posterior convergence.

For Dn∼P0nD_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n},

τ#​Πn⇒QΠ,P0in ​P0n​-probability,\tau_{\#}\Pi_{n}\Rightarrow Q_{\Pi,P_{0}}\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}, (16)

where ⇒\Rightarrow denotes weak convergence of probability laws on ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}. This states that, after the observational law has been learned, the posterior over causal profiles converges to the prior-induced distribution over causal profiles inside ℰΠ​(P0)\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}(P_{0}).

Risk decomposition.

For finite nn, let mn​(Dn)=𝔼Π​[τ⁡(M)∣Dn]m_{n}(D_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\tau(M)\mid D_{n}] and

Vn​(Dn)=𝔼Π​[‖τ⁡(M)−mn​(Dn)‖22∣Dn].V_{n}(D_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\!\left[\|\tau(M)-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}\mid D_{n}\right].

By the squared-loss Pythagorean identity, every measurable estimator f⁡(Dn)f(D_{n}) satisfies

R2​(f)=𝔼⁡[Vn​(Dn)]+𝔼​‖f⁡(Dn)−mn​(Dn)‖22.R_{2}(f)=\mathbb{E}[V_{n}(D_{n})]+\mathbb{E}\|f(D_{n})-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}. (17)

Thus 𝔼​[Vn​(Dn)]\mathbb{E}[V_{n}(D_{n})] is the squared-loss risk that remains after predicting the posterior mean exactly.

Proof.

Condition on Dn=dD_{n}=d and write m⁡(d)=𝔼Π​[τ⁡(M)∣Dn=d]m(d)=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\tau(M)\mid D_{n}=d]. For any vector z∈ℝpz\in\mathbb{R}^{p},

for almost every dataset dd.

τj​(Mπ)=τπ⁡(j)​(M),\tau_{j}(M^{\pi})=\tau_{\pi(j)}(M),

fΠ⋆​(dπ)j\displaystyle f_{\Pi}^{\star}(d^{\pi})_{j} =𝔼Π​[τj​(M)∣Dn=dπ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\tau_{j}(M)\mid D_{n}=d^{\pi}]
=𝔼Π​[τj​(Mπ)∣Dn=d]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\tau_{j}(M^{\pi})\mid D_{n}=d]

Thus

fΠ⋆(Dnπ)j=fΠ⋆(Dn)π⁡(j),j=1,…,p,f_{\Pi}^{\star}(D_{n}^{\pi})_{j}=f_{\Pi}^{\star}(D_{n})_{\pi(j)},\qquad j=1,\ldots,p,

almost surely. ∎

R.6 Proof of Proposition 2

Proof.

Write

Πn(⋅)=Π(⋅∣Dn),Dn∼P0n.\Pi_{n}(\cdot)=\Pi(\cdot\mid D_{n}),\qquad D_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n}.

All convergence statements below are with respect to the sampling law P0nP_{0}^{n}.

Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0. By (A2), there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that, for every M∈𝔐ΠM\in\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi},

dBL​(PM,P0)<δ⟹‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2<ϵ.d_{\mathrm{BL}}(P_{M},P_{0})<\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}<\epsilon.

Thus, on 𝔐Π\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi},

{M:‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2>ϵ}⊆{M:dBL​(PM,P0)≥δ}.\{M:\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}>\epsilon\}\subseteq\{M:d_{\mathrm{BL}}(P_{M},P_{0})\geq\delta\}.

Since Πn​(𝔐Π)=1\Pi_{n}(\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi})=1 for P0nP_{0}^{n}-almost every DnD_{n},

Πn​{M:‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2>ϵ}≤Πn​{M:dBL​(PM,P0)≥δ}\Pi_{n}\{M:\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}>\epsilon\}\leq\Pi_{n}\{M:d_{\mathrm{BL}}(P_{M},P_{0})\geq\delta\}

for P0nP_{0}^{n}-almost every DnD_{n}. The right-hand side converges to zero in P0nP_{0}^{n}-probability by (A1), proving eq. 7.

Now assume also (A3). Let

fΠ,n⋆​(Dn)=∫τ⁡(M)​d​Πn​(M).f_{\Pi,n}^{\star}(D_{n})=\int\tau(M)\,d\Pi_{n}(M).

For any η>0\eta>0,

‖fΠ,n⋆​(Dn)−τ0‖2\displaystyle\|f_{\Pi,n}^{\star}(D_{n})-\tau_{0}\|_{2} =‖∫{τ⁡(M)−τ0}​d​Πn​(M)‖2\displaystyle=\left\|\int\{\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\}\,d\Pi_{n}(M)\right\|_{2}
≤∫‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2​d​Πn​(M)\displaystyle\leq\int\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}\,d\Pi_{n}(M)
≤η+2​B​Πn​{M:‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2>η}.\displaystyle\leq\eta+2B\,\Pi_{n}\{M:\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}>\eta\}.

The final inequality uses (A3) and Πn​(𝔐Π)=1\Pi_{n}(\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi})=1: on 𝔐Π\mathfrak{M}_{\Pi},

‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2≤‖τ⁡(M)‖2+‖τ0‖2≤2​B.\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}\leq\|\tau(M)\|_{2}+\|\tau_{0}\|_{2}\leq 2B.

By eq. 7, the posterior probability in the last display converges to zero in P0nP_{0}^{n}-probability for every fixed η>0\eta>0. Let r>0r>0 and choose η=r/2\eta=r/2. If B=0B=0, then the claim is immediate. Otherwise,

P0n​(‖fΠ,n⋆​(Dn)−τ0‖2>r)\displaystyle P_{0}^{n}\!\left(\|f_{\Pi,n}^{\star}(D_{n})-\tau_{0}\|_{2}>r\right)
≤P0n​(Πn​{M:‖τ⁡(M)−τ0‖2>r/2}>r4​B),\displaystyle\leq P_{0}^{n}\!\left(\Pi_{n}\{M:\|\tau(M)-\tau_{0}\|_{2}>r/2\}>\frac{r}{4B}\right),

which converges to zero by eq. 7. Hence

fΠ,n⋆​(Dn)→τ0in ​P0n​-probability.f_{\Pi,n}^{\star}(D_{n})\to\tau_{0}\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}.

R.8 Non-identifiability and residual causal risk

When the causal profile is not identifiable, infinite observational data reveal P0P_{0} but not which SCM in the equivalence class generated the data. The prior induces a distribution QΠ,P0Q_{\Pi,P_{0}} over causal feature profiles among SCMs observationally equivalent to P0P_{0} (formal disintegration in section R.4). Define τ¯Π​(P0)=∫t​d​QΠ,P0​(t)\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})=\int t\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t) and UΠ​(P0)=∫‖t−τ¯Π​(P0)‖22​d​QΠ,P0​(t)U_{\Pi}(P_{0})=\int\|t-\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t). The causal profile is identifiable at P0P_{0} under the prior exactly when QΠ,P0Q_{\Pi,P_{0}} is a point mass. Then UΠ​(P0)=0U_{\Pi}(P_{0})=0. Otherwise UΠ​(P0)>0U_{\Pi}(P_{0})>0, measuring residual variation in τ⁡(M)\tau(M) among observationally equivalent SCMs.

For finite nn, let mn​(Dn)=𝔼Π​[τ⁡(M)∣Dn]m_{n}(D_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\tau(M)\mid D_{n}] and Vn​(Dn)=𝔼Π​[‖τ⁡(M)−mn​(Dn)‖22∣Dn]V_{n}(D_{n})=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}[\|\tau(M)-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}\mid D_{n}]. The squared-loss Pythagorean identity decomposes ℛ2​(f)=𝔼⁡[Vn​(Dn)]+𝔼​‖f⁡(Dn)−mn​(Dn)‖22\mathcal{R}_{2}(f)=\mathbb{E}[V_{n}(D_{n})]+\mathbb{E}\|f(D_{n})-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}, so 𝔼​[Vn​(Dn)]\mathbb{E}[V_{n}(D_{n})] is the irreducible portion of the risk after predicting the posterior mean exactly (eq. 17). We can now prove the following proposition which characterises the asymptotic behaviour of the Bayes action under non-identifiability – we use an additional regularity assumption (A4), essentially requiring that the prior does not have a discontinuity in how it distributes causal profiles across nearby observational equivalence classes.

Proposition 3 (Limit under non-identifiability).

Assume (A3) and (A4). Then

mn​(Dn)→τ¯Π​(P0),Vn​(Dn)→UΠ​(P0),m_{n}(D_{n})\to\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0}),\qquad V_{n}(D_{n})\to U_{\Pi}(P_{0}), (19)

both in P0nP_{0}^{n}-probability. Moreover, for every observational estimator gn​(Dn)g_{n}(D_{n}), the equivalence-class averaged risk

ℛP0​(gn)=∫𝔼Dn∼P0n​‖gn​(Dn)−t‖22​d​QΠ,P0​(t)\mathcal{R}_{P_{0}}(g_{n})=\int\mathbb{E}_{D_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n}}\|g_{n}(D_{n})-t\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t) (20)

satisfies

ℛP0​(gn)=UΠ​(P0)+𝔼Dn∼P0n​‖gn​(Dn)−τ¯Π​(P0)‖22≥UΠ​(P0).\mathcal{R}_{P_{0}}(g_{n})=U_{\Pi}(P_{0})+\mathbb{E}_{D_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n}}\|g_{n}(D_{n})-\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})\|_{2}^{2}\geq U_{\Pi}(P_{0}). (21)

Thus, in non-identifiable regimes, the posterior mean converges to the prior-weighted mean of the causal profiles compatible with P0P_{0}. This is the squared-loss Bayes action under the pretraining prior, but it need not equal the causal profile of any particular SCM in the equivalence class compatible with P0P_{0}.

Example: Two observationally equivalent SCMs.

Suppose M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} satisfy PM1=PM2=P0P_{M_{1}}=P_{M_{2}}=P_{0}, but t1=τ⁡(M1)≠t2=τ⁡(M2)t_{1}=\tau(M_{1})\neq t_{2}=\tau(M_{2}). For any estimator gn​(Dn)g_{n}(D_{n}) based only on observational samples,

maxk∈{1,2}⁡𝔼Dn∼P0n​‖gn​(Dn)−tk‖22≥14​‖t1−t2‖22.\max_{k\in\{1,2\}}\mathbb{E}_{D_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n}}\|g_{n}(D_{n})-t_{k}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\|t_{1}-t_{2}\|_{2}^{2}. (22)

If the prior assigns equal mass to M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}, then τ¯Π​(P0)=(t1+t2)/2\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})=(t_{1}+t_{2})/2 and UΠ​(P0)=14​‖t1−t2‖22U_{\Pi}(P_{0})=\frac{1}{4}\|t_{1}-t_{2}\|_{2}^{2}, so the posterior mean attains eq. 22 in the equivalence-class averaged sense.

The one-dimensional instance of this example is illustrated in Fig. 9 and Table 28. Let M1M_{1} be X→YX\to Y with standardized effect τX=2​ρ\tau_{X}=2\rho, and let M2M_{2} be Y→XY\to X with τX=0\tau_{X}=0. These SCMs have the same observational covariance but different intervention effects. With equal prior weights, the posterior mean is ρ\rho, and the residual squared error is ρ2\rho^{2}. For ρ=0.6\rho=0.6, this gives 0.360.36, matching the no-free-lunch value in Table 28. Disagreement under hidden confounding, Gaussian direction ambiguity, or other observational equivalences is therefore not merely a failure of amortization or optimization. It is a limitation of the information available in DnD_{n}. A method can resolve it only by adding identifying assumptions through the prior, observing interventions, or abstaining.

R.9 Proof of Proposition  3

Proof.

Let

Qn​(Dn)=τ#​ΠnQ_{n}(D_{n})=\tau_{\#}\Pi_{n}

denote the posterior distribution of the causal feature profile. Then

mn​(Dn)=∫t​d​Qn​(t),Vn​(Dn)=∫‖t−mn​(Dn)‖22​d​Qn​(t).m_{n}(D_{n})=\int t\,dQ_{n}(t),\qquad V_{n}(D_{n})=\int\|t-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{n}(t).

We first record the squared-loss decomposition. For any measurable estimator f⁡(Dn)f(D_{n}), conditioning on DnD_{n} gives

𝔼⁡[‖f⁡(Dn)−τ⁡(M)‖22∣Dn]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|f(D_{n})-\tau(M)\|_{2}^{2}\mid D_{n}\right] =𝔼⁡[‖f⁡(Dn)−mn​(Dn)+mn​(Dn)−τ⁡(M)‖22∣Dn]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|f(D_{n})-m_{n}(D_{n})+m_{n}(D_{n})-\tau(M)\|_{2}^{2}\mid D_{n}\right]
=‖f⁡(Dn)−mn​(Dn)‖22+𝔼⁡[‖τ⁡(M)−mn​(Dn)‖22∣Dn],\displaystyle=\|f(D_{n})-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\tau(M)-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}\mid D_{n}\right],

because

𝔼⁡[τ⁡(M)−mn​(Dn)∣Dn]=0.\mathbb{E}[\tau(M)-m_{n}(D_{n})\mid D_{n}]=0.

Taking expectations proves

R2​(f)=𝔼⁡[Vn​(Dn)]+𝔼​‖f⁡(Dn)−mn​(Dn)‖22.R_{2}(f)=\mathbb{E}[V_{n}(D_{n})]+\mathbb{E}\|f(D_{n})-m_{n}(D_{n})\|_{2}^{2}.

We next prove the two convergence claims in eq. 19. By (A3), both Qn​(Dn)Q_{n}(D_{n}) and QΠ,P0Q_{\Pi,P_{0}} are supported on the closed Euclidean ball {t:‖t‖2≤B}\{t:\|t\|_{2}\leq B\} for P0nP_{0}^{n}-almost every DnD_{n}. Weak convergence in (A4) on a bounded support gives convergence of the first and second moments. Hence

∫tj​d​Qn​(t)→∫tj​d​QΠ,P0​(t)in ​P0n​-probability\int t_{j}\,dQ_{n}(t)\to\int t_{j}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t)\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}

for every jj, and therefore

mn​(Dn)=∫t​d​Qn​(t)→∫t​d​QΠ,P0​(t)=τ¯Π​(P0)in ​P0n​-probability.m_{n}(D_{n})=\int t\,dQ_{n}(t)\to\int t\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t)=\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}.

Similarly, the map t↦‖t‖22t\mapsto\|t\|_{2}^{2} is bounded and Lipschitz on the ball {t:‖t‖2≤B}\{t:\|t\|_{2}\leq B\}. Thus

∫‖t‖22​d​Qn​(t)→∫‖t‖22​d​QΠ,P0​(t)in ​P0n​-probability.\int\|t\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{n}(t)\to\int\|t\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t)\quad\text{in }P_{0}^{n}\text{-probability}.

Using

Vn​(Dn)=∫‖t‖22​d​Qn​(t)−‖∫t​d​Qn​(t)‖22V_{n}(D_{n})=\int\|t\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{n}(t)-\left\|\int t\,dQ_{n}(t)\right\|_{2}^{2}

and the convergence of the first moment just proved, we obtain

Vn​(Dn)→∫‖t‖22​d​QΠ,P0​(t)−‖∫t​d​QΠ,P0​(t)‖22=UΠ​(P0)V_{n}(D_{n})\to\int\|t\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t)-\left\|\int t\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t)\right\|_{2}^{2}=U_{\Pi}(P_{0})

in P0nP_{0}^{n}-probability.

It remains to prove eq. 21. For any fixed vector a∈ℝpa\in\mathbb{R}^{p},

∫‖a−t‖22​d​QΠ,P0​(t)\displaystyle\int\|a-t\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t) =∫‖a−τ¯Π​(P0)+τ¯Π​(P0)−t‖22​d​QΠ,P0​(t)\displaystyle=\int\|a-\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})+\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})-t\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t)
=‖a−τ¯Π​(P0)‖22+∫‖t−τ¯Π​(P0)‖22​d​QΠ,P0​(t),\displaystyle=\|a-\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})\|_{2}^{2}+\int\|t-\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})\|_{2}^{2}\,dQ_{\Pi,P_{0}}(t),

Substituting a=gn​(Dn)a=g_{n}(D_{n}) and taking expectation over Dn∼P0nD_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n} gives

ℛP0​(gn)=UΠ​(P0)+𝔼Dn∼P0n​‖gn​(Dn)−τ¯Π​(P0)‖22≥UΠ​(P0),\mathcal{R}_{P_{0}}(g_{n})=U_{\Pi}(P_{0})+\mathbb{E}_{D_{n}\sim P_{0}^{n}}\|g_{n}(D_{n})-\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})\|_{2}^{2}\geq U_{\Pi}(P_{0}),

as claimed.

For the Example with two observationally equivalent SCMs, since PM1=PM2=P0P_{M_{1}}=P_{M_{2}}=P_{0}, the distribution of gn​(Dn)g_{n}(D_{n}) is the same whether the data are generated from M1M_{1} or from M2M_{2}. Let GG denote a random vector with this common distribution, and write tk=τ⁡(Mk)t_{k}=\tau(M_{k}) for k=1,2k=1,2. Then

𝔼​‖G−t1‖22+𝔼​‖G−t2‖22\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|G-t_{1}\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|G-t_{2}\|_{2}^{2} =2​𝔼​‖G−t1+t22‖22+12​‖t1−t2‖22.\displaystyle=2\mathbb{E}\left\|G-\frac{t_{1}+t_{2}}{2}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|t_{1}-t_{2}\|_{2}^{2}.

=𝔼​‖G−t1+t22‖22+14​‖t1−t2‖22\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left\|G-\frac{t_{1}+t_{2}}{2}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\|t_{1}-t_{2}\|_{2}^{2}
≥14​‖t1−t2‖22.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{4}\|t_{1}-t_{2}\|_{2}^{2}.

If the prior assigns equal mass to M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}, then the induced equivalence-class distribution is

QΠ,P0=12​δt1+12​δt2.Q_{\Pi,P_{0}}=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{t_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{t_{2}}.

Hence

τ¯Π​(P0)=t1+t22,\bar{\tau}_{\Pi}(P_{0})=\frac{t_{1}+t_{2}}{2},

=14​‖t1−t2‖22.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\|t_{1}-t_{2}\|_{2}^{2}.
